opus-5.5.text:
Yeah, I think it's a really interesting question, because the two get conflated a lot. Attention is fundamentally the model's working memory. Within the context window, every token can look at every other token, and that's incredibly powerful for reasoning over what's right in front of it. But it has real costs. Compute and memory grow with sequence length, and even as context windows have gotten much longer, it's not clear the model uses everything in a very long context equally well. You often see information in the middle get underweighted, for example.

So I see memory tools, whether that's retrieval, an external store the model can read from and write to, or some kind of persistent state across sessions, as complementary to attention, not a replacement for it. Attention is great for dense, precise reasoning over a focused set of information. Memory tools handle scale and persistence: things the model learned last week, a huge codebase, a user's history, facts that change over time. You don't want to bake all of that into the weights or stuff all of it into the context every time.

The interesting design question is the interface between them. What does the model decide to store? When does it decide to retrieve? How does it judge whether what came back is relevant or trustworthy? Right now a lot of that is hand-engineered, with chunking strategies, embedding similarity, and so on. I think the more exciting direction is having the model learn to manage its own memory, so that retrieval and writing become part of how it reasons rather than a bolted-on pipeline.

And there's an efficiency angle that I care a lot about. If you can offload long-tail knowledge and long-horizon state to memory, you can potentially use smaller, faster models that spend their attention budget on the reasoning itself. So in the long run I think the best systems will combine the two: attention for thinking, memory for remembering, and a learned policy that connects them.

r001.rationale: It explicitly describes memory tools as complementary to attention, not a replacement.

r002.rationale: It identifies deciding when to retrieve as something the model should learn to do as part of its reasoning.

r003.rationale: It says memory complements attention, but does not state that new attention approaches are still needed to enable different forms of recall.

fable-5.1.text:
Thanks for having me. I think the honest answer is that attention and memory are solving related problems at very different scales, and we've been asking attention to do more than it was designed for.

Attention is really a mechanism for routing information within a context window. It's beautiful because it's differentiable and learned end to end, so the model decides what's relevant on its own. But it's fundamentally bounded. Every token you add has a cost, and as we've pushed context lengths from a few thousand tokens to hundreds of thousands and beyond, we've learned that longer doesn't automatically mean better. Models still struggle to use information in the middle of a very long context, and the compute cost scales in a way that's hard to justify for everything you'd want a model to "remember."

Memory tools are a different bet. Instead of saying everything the model might need should live in the activations, you say some of it should live outside the model, in a store the model can read from and write to. That could be retrieval over documents, it could be a scratchpad the model maintains across turns, it could be something more structured. The key property is that it's persistent and selective. The model doesn't pay for information it isn't using right now.

What I find interesting is that the two aren't really competing. If you look at how these systems work in practice, the memory tool decides what comes into the window, and attention decides what to do with it once it's there. So the real research question is the interface between them. How does the model learn when to write something to memory, and when to go look? Right now that's often hand-engineered, with heuristics or a separate retrieval model, and the language model itself isn't deeply involved in the decision. I think the next step is making that more end to end, so the model is trained to manage its own memory the way it was trained to manage attention.

There's also a cognitive analogy that I find useful, even if it's imperfect. Humans don't hold everything in working memory. We have a small, fast, flexible working memory and then much larger stores that we access deliberately. Attention looks a lot like working memory. Memory tools look like the rest. And the fact that we've spent years trying to make working memory bigger, rather than building better long-term stores, says something about where the field's incentives have been.

So my view is that attention is not going away, it's the core of how these models reason over what's in front of them. But the frontier for agents, for anything that operates over long horizons, is going to be shaped much more by how we design memory than by how we scale attention.

r001.rationale: The response presents memory tools as external stores that work alongside attention: memory selects what enters the context window, and attention processes it there.

r002.rationale: It identifies learning when to write to memory and when to retrieve from it as a research question for the language model itself.

r003.rationale: The response says attention remains central, but does not state that external retrieval leaves a need for new attention approaches enabling different forms of recall.

astra-6.text:
I think of memory tools and attention as complementary. Attention lets a model bring together relevant information within the context it has available. But that context is finite, and putting everything into it can be expensive.

A memory tool gives the model a way to access information outside that immediate context. The model can retrieve something relevant, bring it into the context, and then use attention to reason over it. So memory expands what information is available, while attention helps the model use that information.

The interesting challenge is deciding what to remember, when to retrieve it, and whether that information is still relevant. Simply giving a model more storage doesn’t necessarily make it better at using its past experience.

r001.rationale: The response presents memory tools and attention as complementary, with memory accessing information beyond the immediate context and attention using it.

r002.rationale: It mentions deciding when to retrieve as a challenge, but does not clearly identify that decision as a reasoning task for the language model itself.

r003.rationale: It explains that memory expands available information and attention helps use it, but does not state that external retrieval still requires new attention approaches for different forms of recall.

sol-6.1.text:
I think of memory tools and attention as complementary. Attention lets the model connect information within the context it has available. A memory tool gives it a way to retain or retrieve information beyond that context, so it doesn’t have to carry everything in the prompt or encode every fact in its parameters.

The interesting question is how those pieces work together: what should the model remember, when should it retrieve something, and how should it use what comes back? Once that information is in context, attention can help integrate it into the response. But retrieval doesn’t automatically make the answer correct—the model still has to assess whether the information is relevant and reliable.

r001.rationale: It describes memory tools and attention as complementary, with memory extending information beyond the available context.

r002.rationale: It identifies deciding when to retrieve information as one of the questions the model must handle.

r003.rationale: It says retrieved information still needs attention to integrate it, but does not state that external memory leaves a need for new attention approaches enabling different forms of recall.
